NeurIPS 2025 — 39th Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems

03 · Insights

Paper-by-paper tech insights

A · Self-verifying reasoning & code
01

Trust, But Verify: Self-Verifying RL (RISE)

Xiaoyuan Liu et al. · CUHK, Shenzhen
Goal

Teach a model to check its own reasoning during training, instead of relying on a separate verifier.

Challenge

LLMs reason fluently but can’t reliably tell when they are wrong; an external verifier adds cost, complexity and instability.

Method
  • Roll out chain-of-thought solutions to a batch of problems
  • Turn each solution into a verification task via a template
  • Jointly train reasoning and verification with RL (RISE)
Novelty

Goes past shallow ‘self-reflection’ — reasoning and checking are learned together in one RL loop.

Impact

Models that audit their own answers — safer AI for code, education and decision support where wrong reasoning is costly.

Code · github.com/xyliu-cs/RISE
[1] X. Liu et al., “Trust, But Verify: A Self-Verification Approach to Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards,” NeurIPS 2025.
02

Rethinking Verification for LLM Code Generation (SAGA)

Zihan Ma et al. · Shanghai AI Laboratory
Goal

Judge an LLM’s code by the strength of the tests, not the size of the model.

Challenge

AI coding tools hide subtle logic bugs because existing test suites and verifiers miss edge cases.

Method
  • Define metrics for test-suite strength (detection rate, verifier accuracy)
  • Generate stronger, more diverse tests with a human–LLM loop grounded on a trusted solution
Novelty

Identifies test-suite strength — not model size — as the real limiter of reliable code generation.

Impact

Stronger QA pipelines, safer AI coding products, and standard metrics for benchmarking reliability.

Code · github.com/open-compass/SAGA
[2] Z. Ma et al., “Rethinking Verification for LLM Code Generation: From Generation to Testing,” NeurIPS 2025.
B · Efficient, knowledge-aware agents
03

GAP: Graph-Based Agent Planning with Parallel Tools

Jiaqi Wu et al. · Tsinghua University
Goal

Let a single agent run independent tool calls in parallel instead of one after another.

Challenge

Sequential LLM agents are slow and costly on multi-step tasks; multi-agent setups add coordination overhead.

Method
  • Build a dependency graph (DAG) of sub-tasks
  • Run independent branches in parallel; use RL to learn when to parallelize
Novelty

Parallelism without the complexity of multi-agent systems — one agent that learns task dependencies.

Impact

Lower latency, fewer tokens and cheaper tool-augmented workflows — good for real-world deployment.

Code · github.com/WJQ7777/Graph-Agent-Planning
[3] J. Wu et al., “GAP: Graph-based Agent Planning with Parallel Tool Use and Reinforcement Learning,” NeurIPS 2025.
04

RAG4GFM: Retrieval-Augmented Graph Foundation Models

Xingliang Wang et al. · Zhejiang University
Goal

Keep graph foundation models up to date without retraining them.

Challenge

Graph models are expensive to retrain and hallucinate structure as the underlying graph data changes.

Method
  • Build a multi-level graph index (node, edge, graph features)
  • Retrieve the most relevant subgraphs per task type
  • Fuse them with the query graph by features and topology
Novelty

Injects fresh knowledge at inference with structure-aware retrieval — O(log N) lookup instead of retraining.

Impact

Adaptive, low-cost, always-updated graph intelligence for fraud detection, recommendations and dynamic knowledge.

Code · github.com/Matrixmax/RAG4GFM
[4] X. Wang et al., “RAG4GFM: Bridging Knowledge Gaps in Graph Foundation Models through Graph Retrieval Augmented Generation,” NeurIPS 2025.
C · Reliability, safety & security
05

Reliable LLM-Robot Planning via Uncertainty (CURE)

Shiyuan Yin et al. · Henan University of Technology
Goal

Give LLM-driven robots a trustworthy sense of when a plan is risky.

Challenge

Robots can’t safely decide whether to act or ask when their uncertainty signals are unreliable.

Method
  • Split uncertainty into epistemic (knowledge gaps) and intrinsic (randomness)
  • Gauge familiarity with RND novelty detection; combine into one risk score
Novelty

Separates uncertainty into clarity, familiarity and unpredictability — a structured, planner-agnostic layer.

Impact

A plug-and-play safety layer so robots act or ask appropriately — more dependable home and factory automation.

Code · github.com/Firesuiry/CURE
[5] S. Yin et al., “Towards Reliable LLM-based Robots Planning via Combined Uncertainty Estimation,” NeurIPS 2025.
06

Safe + Safe = Unsafe? Jailbreaking VLMs with Safe Images

Chenhang Cui et al. · National University of Singapore
Goal

Show that even safe images can be chained together to jailbreak vision-language models.

Challenge

Safety work focuses on obviously harmful inputs; benign images are a blind spot.

Method
  • Pair safe images with gentle questions
  • Escalate over multiple turns and watch for unsafe reasoning
  • Measure how often models ‘snowball’ and analyze why
Novelty

A realistic black-box attack using only safe images — exposing risks from the model’s own reasoning.

Impact

Calls for cross-modal consistency checks, multi-turn self-evaluation and safe-input red-teaming benchmarks.

Code · github.com/gzcch/Safety_Snowball_Agent
[6] C. Cui et al., “Safe + Safe = Unsafe? Exploring How Safe Images Can Be Exploited to Jailbreak Large Vision-Language Models,” NeurIPS 2025.
07

DRIFT: Dynamic Defense for Securing LLM Agents

Hao Li et al. · Washington University
Goal

Defend LLM agents against prompt injection without crippling their usefulness.

Challenge

Static defenses are inflexible and fail on new attacks; model-level safeguards miss unseen injections.

Method
  • Secure Planner builds a minimal action plan + parameter checklist
  • Dynamic Validator flags deviations; Injection Isolator masks malicious instructions
Novelty

Enforces control- and data-level rules dynamically, adapting policies in real time.

Impact

Safer, flexible agent deployments — beats fixed-rule systems (e.g. CaMeL) on adaptability vs. protection.

Code · github.com/SaFoLab-WISC/DRIFT
[7] H. Li et al., “DRIFT: Dynamic Rule-Based Defense with Injection Isolation for Securing LLM Agents,” NeurIPS 2025.
04 · Conclusions

Synthesis across the papers

Insights

  • Reliability, verification and interpretability are now first-class goals, not afterthoughts.
  • Agents are getting structured — dependency graphs, retrieval and self-checking replace brute force.
  • Safety must be cross-modal and dynamic; even ‘safe’ inputs and new injections are threats.

Vision

  • AI that reasons more deliberately and checks its own work.
  • Compute- and energy-efficient architectures for sustainable training and serving.
  • Standard metrics and benchmarks for trust, not just accuracy.

Implications for us

  • Invest in self-verifying reasoning and stronger test / verification pipelines.
  • Adopt parallel, retrieval-augmented agents to cut latency and cost.
  • Add adaptive, cross-modal safety and injection defenses to agent products.
